transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
- Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Lyndi Kenyon.
President Trump's campaign push ahead of the midterms
took him to northwest Georgia yesterday
where he rallied on behalf of Republican Senate nominee
Congressman Mike Collins.
He also repeated false claims about the 2020 elections.
Rahul Bali of member station WABE has the story.
Trump bounced from topic to topic
during his roughly 90 minute speech
that included several attacks on U.S. Senator John Ossoff,
the only Democratic Senator up for reelection this year
in a state Trump won in 2024.
- He does not represent your values
and he never won the election.
He was in there as an impostor.
- Trump referring to the 2020 elections
which he continues to falsely claim he won in Georgia
along with falsely claiming
that then Senator David Perdue won rather than Ossoff.
The president stopped short of making any claims
on election security related to this year.
For NPR News, I'm Rahul Bali in Dalton, Georgia.
- Candidates for Iowa's open U.S. Senate seat
are campaigning across the state.
Iowa Public Radio's Natalie Krebs
reports they're making a push for votes
in a highly competitive race,
one of the several that could determine
control of the U.S. Senate.
Republican Congresswoman Ashley Hinton
and Democratic seat lawmaker Josh Turrick
are vying for retiring Republican Senator Joni Ernst's seat.
Polling indicates the race is a toss-up.
At a recent event for Hinton in suburban Des Moines,
voter Kathy Jenkins says she's concerned
about immigration and the war in Iran.
- I mean, yes, our gas prices up,
but hey, if we can keep Iran from a nuclear weapon,
I'm all about it.
I've got grandchildren and I want them
to have the same, live in the same country that I do.
- Early voting in Iowa started this week.
For NPR News, I'm Natalie Krebs in Des Moines.
- It was a mixed week on Wall Street
as inflation continues to cause headaches.
NPR's Scott Horsley reports blue chips were up for the week,
but the broader market was down.
- Reports this week from the Labor Department
showed prices climbing faster
than forecasters expected in September.
Inflation's been outpacing wage gains in recent months,
but shoppers continue to open their wallets.
The National Retail Federation says it expects holiday sales
to grow more than 4% this year to just over a trillion dollars.
On Friday, the Treasury Department said
the federal deficit for the just-ended fiscal year
was nearly $2 trillion.
The government's borrowing so much money,
it's putting upward pressure on interest rates
for everyone else.
For the week, the Dow Jones Industrial Average
rose 2/3 of a percent, but the S&P 500 index fell nearly 2%,
and the NASDAQ tumbled 4 1/2%.
Scott Horsley, NPR News, Washington.
- Pope Leo has been discharged from the hospital
after lung cancer surgery.
The Vatican says the Pope plans to deliver
traditional noon prayers tomorrow in St. Peter's Square.
You're listening to NPR.
Authorities in England held an emergency summit this week
to discuss a climate-related phenomenon,
a huge number of octopuses multiplying in British waters.
NPR's Lauren Frayer reports from London.
- Fishers and scientists are trying to cope
with what they call an octopus bloom,
a nearly 1,500% increase in octopus caught off the coast
of southwest England over the past five years.
Warming sea temperatures mean the animals
are migrating farther north from Europe.
For some in England's fishing industry, it's a boon.
They're exporting record numbers to France and Spain,
where octopus is more common on menus.
But shellfish here have been decimated
because octopus eat crabs, lobsters, clams, and mussels.
Businesses that farmer catch those creatures
have been hit hard.
Animal welfare groups meanwhile caution
against the exploitation
of these intelligent sentient creatures.
Lauren Frayer, NPR News, London.
- Think of it as a much needed distraction
from the ongoing war that has engulfed Gaza in recent years.
Big muscle men took part in the Palestine
strongman championship yesterday.
It featured big burly men pulling trucks with ropes,
flipping massive tires,
doing all those things that we see in such competitions
in other parts of the world.
Spectators watched against the backdrop of rubble
from buildings destroyed in the war.
The strongman championship was postponed for years
due to the war with Israel.
I'm Linda Kenyon.
NPR News in Washington.

topics.text: Trump rallies in northwest Georgia for Mike Collins, repeats false 2020 election claims
Iowa Senate candidates Ashley Hinton and Josh Turek campaign in tight race for Ernst's seat
Wall Street mixed for the week as inflation rises faster than expected in September
Pope Leo discharged from hospital after lung cancer surgery, plans noon prayers at St. Peter's
England holds emergency summit on octopus bloom multiplying in British waters
Palestine strongman championship held in Gaza amid rubble from the war
